summary: Describes sampling and filtering techniques for choosing which IP packets to look at, categorizes the common schemes, and lists the parameters needed to describe them. It also shows how simple selection methods can be combined into more elaborate ones. It provides the basis for the PSAMP work.

eli5.summary: Checking every single packet can be too much work, so you pick some. This note describes ways to pick them, such as every tenth one or a random few, and how to mix those methods.

questions: how to select ip packets for measurement
subtitle: A catalogue of ways a router can pick a manageable subset of packets to measure, and what each one needs to be described.

tldr.problem: Network speeds and the appetite for fine-grained measurement produce more data than can be captured, stored and processed, and capturing everything at line rate with specialised hardware is too costly to be ubiquitous.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits packet selection into Sampling (picking a representative subset by position, time or chance) and Filtering (deterministic selection by packet content or router state, including hash-based selection), then lists the parameters that describe each scheme and how to combine them.
tldr.outcome: It is the selection-technique basis of the PSAMP work, and it requires the BOB hash function for hash-based selection, while warning that none of the listed hash functions stops a determined attacker.

facts.label: Crypto hash slowdown
facts.value: about 7-10 times for MD5 and SHA

today: RFC 5475 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sits alongside RFC 5474, RFC 5476 and RFC 5477.

sections.title: Why Select Packets at All
sections.content:
Two trends drive this work: network data rates keep rising, and measurement applications want ever finer-grained data. Together they create an overwhelming amount of measurement data, with high demands on resources for measurement, storage, transfer and post-processing.

Specialised hardware can capture traffic at line rate, but its cost and the infrastructure around it rule it out as a ubiquitous approach. Some form of data reduction at the point of measurement is therefore necessary.

The RFC covers two kinds of packet selection. Sampling aims to choose a representative subset so that properties of the unsampled traffic can be estimated accurately. Filtering removes all packets that are not of interest. Aggregation, a third way to cut data, is out of scope. This document is one of a series from the PSAMP group, alongside the framework (RFC 5474), the protocol (RFC 5476) and the information model (RFC 5477).
sections.eli5: Writing down every single thing that happens is too much work, so you pick which things to write down. This note lists the sensible ways to pick.

sections.title: The Selection Vocabulary
sections.content:
An Observation Point is a place where packets can be seen, such as a line, a shared medium, a router port or an embedded subsystem within an interface. All packets seen there form the Observed Packet Stream.

A Selection Process takes that stream as input and outputs a subset. It is built from Selectors, each deciding for a single packet using the Packet Content, how the packet was treated at the Observation Point, or any Selection State the process keeps (such as sequence numbers, timestamps, pseudorandom number iterators or hash values). A Composite Selector chains Selectors so one's output feeds the next. A Primitive Selector is any Selector that is not composite.

A Metering Process uses a Selection Process to produce a Report Stream of Packet Reports. It is analogous to the IPFIX Metering Process (RFC 5101), except that a PSAMP Metering Process always contains a Selection Process. An Exporting Process sends the reports to a Collector.

Several size terms recur. The Configured Selection Fraction is the expected ratio of Sample Size to Population Size, from the configuration. The Attained Selection Fraction is the actual ratio, which can differ because of statistical variability.
sections.eli5: A Selector is a gatekeeper that decides yes or no for each packet. You can line gatekeepers up in a row, and what passes the first one goes to the next.

sections.title: Sampling Versus Filtering
sections.content:
The RFC draws a sharp line. Sampling picks a representative subset to learn about the whole. The choice can depend on packet position, on Packet Content, or on random decisions. Filtering picks a subset with common properties because only that subset is of interest. It is deterministic, and never depends on packet position or randomness.

Hashing is the awkward case. A hash is a deterministic function of the Packet Content, so by this categorisation it is Filtering, yet hash functions are often used to imitate random Sampling with a given probability p. It also lets several Observation Points consistently select the same packets.

The RFC adds that this split is mainly useful for describing Primitive Selectors. More complex practices, such as weighting selection probability by packet length, can be described as a cascade of Filtering and Sampling. If a common practice is too complex for that, an ad hoc description may be added as a new scheme.
sections.eli5: Sampling is like picking a few people at random to guess what everyone thinks. Filtering is like only talking to people wearing a blue hat. Hashing follows a fixed rule, so it counts as the blue-hat kind, even though it can look random.

sections.title: Sampling Schemes
sections.content:
Systematic sampling uses a deterministic function to choose where selection intervals start and how long they last, for example every k-th packet or all packets arriving at predefined times. It can be count-based or time-based. Its risk is bias: if the pattern resembles a pattern in the traffic, the estimate is likely to be biased.

Random sampling chooses starting points by a random process and can give unbiased estimates, but needs random numbers. It has two forms. In n-out-of-N sampling, n packets are selected out of a Population of N, so the Sample Size is fixed. In probabilistic sampling each packet is selected according to a predefined probability, so the Sample Size can vary between trials.

Probabilistic sampling is uniform when every packet has the same probability p. Counted in packets this is geometric random sampling, and its time-driven analog is exponential random sampling. It is non-uniform when the probability depends on the input, for instance to boost rare but important packets, with unbiased estimates recovered by re-normalising sample values.

A further type is flow-state dependent sampling, used with an IPFIX flow monitor. In the "sample and hold" method, a packet that matches an existing Flow Record is selected, and one that does not is selected with probability p and then creates a new Flow Record. The RFC leaves concrete non-uniform schemes and their parameters to vendors.
sections.eli5: You can count every tenth car, or roll a die for each car. The die way is fairer if the traffic has a pattern. You can also keep a close eye on cars you have already noticed.

sections.title: Filtering and Hash-Based Selection
sections.content:
Property match filtering selects a packet if a field, or a property of router state, equals a predefined value (Field=Value). Fields come from the IPFIX attributes in RFC 5102, from the IP header, transport header or encapsulation headers such as an MPLS label stack. Router state can include the ingress or egress interface, an ACL violation, a failed reverse path forwarding check, a failed RSVP check, no route found, or the origin or destination BGP autonomous system. Filters can be ANDed by chaining them, but OR is not supported in the basic model. Filtering must be configurable to ignore encrypted packets.

Hash-based selection applies a hash function to part of the Packet Content (the Hash Domain) and selects the packet if the result falls in a Hash Selection Range, a subset of the Hash Range. Its main use is coordinated selection: every Observation Point using the same function and parameters picks the same packets. The input fields should be invariant along the path and variable among packets, which excludes fields such as Time-to-Live and the header checksum.

Uses of coordinated selection include trajectory sampling (reconstructing a packet's path from reports, which helps estimate path matrices, detect routing loops, measure loss and one-way delay, and trace attack packets with spoofed source addresses) and passive one-way delay measurement. Hash outputs can also serve as a cheap source of pseudorandom numbers.
sections.eli5: Filtering is a bouncer with a checklist. Hash-based picking is a bouncer who scrambles each guest's details into a number and lets in anyone whose number lands in a chosen range. Every door that uses the same scrambling picks the same guests.

sections.title: Choosing a Hash Function
sections.content:
Good hash functions for selection are fast, mix well (small input changes cause large output changes), are unbiased, give a representative sample, are non-linear and resist attacks. For packet digests, a low collision rate and variable-length input matter more than speed.

The ideal is a cryptographically strong function with a private parameter in pseudorandom function mode, but the RFC admits that no single function meets every requirement, and that MD5 and SHA computation times were about 7-10 times higher than non-cryptographic functions. So the functions it standardises are weaker.

  • If hash-based selection is used, the BOB function MUST be used for packet selection to be PSAMP compliant. Its initial vector MUST be configurable out of band, and both the init value and the selection range should be kept private.
  • Other functions, such as CRC-32 and IPSX, MAY be used. IPSX is about an order of magnitude faster, but limited to 16 bytes of input.
  • For packet digesting, BOB SHOULD be used and others such as CRC-32 MAY be. IPSX is not recommended there because of its higher collision rate.

For IPv4, BOB MUST be fed the IP identification, flags, fragment offset, source and destination addresses and a configurable number of payload bytes. For IPv6 it MUST use the payload length, bytes 10, 11, 14, 15 and 16 of each address, and a configurable number of payload bytes (at least 4 recommended). Evaluations were done only for IPv4.
sections.eli5: A good scrambler turns similar-looking inputs into very different numbers. The strongest scramblers are slow, so this note picks a quicker one called BOB and warns that it is not unbreakable.

sections.title: Describing and Combining Selectors
sections.content:
To comply with PSAMP, at least one of the described schemes MUST be implemented. Each Sampler or Filter is described by three things: a SELECTOR_ID (unique ID), a SELECTOR_TYPE and SELECTOR_PARAMETERS.

  • Systematic count-based: interval length and spacing in packets.
  • Systematic time-based: interval length and spacing in microseconds.
  • n-out-of-N: Population Size N and Sample Size n.
  • Uniform probabilistic: the Sampling probability p.
  • Matching filters: an Information Element and a value, with multiple criteria joined by logical AND.
  • Hashing filters: Hash Domain, Hash Function, output length and a Hash Selection Range given as non-overlapping intervals. For example, ranges [1:3] and [6:9] select hash results 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8 and 9.

Composite schemes are described by a Selection Sequence, the ordered list of Selector IDs applied to the stream. Putting a filter before a sampler lets each filtered stream have its own sampling rate, but if filters are too complex to run at full line rate, sampling before filtering may be needed. Stratified sampling groups the Population by a correlated characteristic using filters and then samples each group, which can improve accuracy or cut the sample size needed.
sections.eli5: Every picking rule gets a name tag and a small settings card, such as pick every tenth. You can chain rules together, with the order mattering for speed.

sections.title: Attacks on Selection
sections.content:
A concern with hash-based selection is that a set of related packets could be disproportionately sampled, whether by unexpected function behaviour or by crafted packets. The RFC assumes the hash function is public. Without a private parameter, an attacker can craft packets with known selection outcomes. A non-cryptographic function such as CRC-32 can remain exploitable even with a private modulus. If the attacker can learn selection outcomes, for example from billing reports, intrusion detection feedback or by watching the Report Stream, a modular hash can be broken with knowledge of roughly 2/p outcomes.

Because hash selection is deterministic, known packets can be replayed with the same outcome unless parameters change. Changing them regularly helps, but trajectory sampling needs the change to be simultaneous across Observation Points. Only a cryptographic hash with a private parameter in pseudorandom function mode withstands these attacks, and the RFC states that BOB and CRC-32 are not recommended for cryptographic purposes.

Time-based systematic sampling can be learned by sending test packets, and random sampling should use a cryptographically strong random number generator. Threats to configuring and reporting sampling parameters are out of scope.
sections.eli5: If a sneaky person learns your picking rule, they can make their packets always get picked or always get skipped. Changing the rule often and keeping part of it secret makes that harder.
